chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn Hadid, from some of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
The oaths are three: an oath for which there is no expiation, an oath in which there is an expiation, and a calamitous (false) oath that obligates the Fire.
The oath for which there is no expiation is the man swearing by God upon a matter of righteousness that he will not do it — his expiation is that he does it.
And the oath in which expiation is obligated is the man swearing upon a matter of disobedience that he will not do it, then he does it — expiation becomes obligated upon him.
And the calamitous (false) oath that obligates the Fire is the man swearing upon the right of a Muslim person to withhold his wealth.

key_terms.الأيمان: Plural of yamīn, oaths/sworn pledges. In jurisprudence, specifically oaths taken in God's name.
key_terms.الكفارة: Expiation or atonement; the prescribed act (feeding the poor, fasting, or freeing a slave) performed to atone for a broken oath.
key_terms.بر: Righteousness, piety, and good deeds. An act of birr is a virtuous or charitable act.
key_terms.غموس: Literally 'submerging/plunging'; used for a deliberately false oath that plunges its taker into sin and hellfire.

ai.seo_question: What are the three types of oaths in Islam according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) classifies oaths into three legal categories: (1) an oath to omit a righteous act, which is expiated by performing it; (2) an oath to avoid sin that is broken, requiring formal expiation (kaffarah); and (3) the yamīn al-ghamus (literally 'the submerging oath'), a deliberately false oath sworn to seize another person's wealth, for which there is no expiation — only the punishment of the Fire. This typology reflects the classical Shia fiqh understanding that the gravity of an oath is determined by its subject matter and whether it involves deliberate fraud against another's rights. The yamīn al-ghamus was a serious social problem in Arabian society where oath-taking was used to fraudulently deny others their legitimate claims.
